messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

John, a 65-year-old widowed man of Oceania descent, has been navigating his life with profound difficulty ever since his son was hospitalized for a severe and life-threatening illness three years ago. John’s experience during that time has left him grappling with an array of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily functioning as a project manager and his overall well-being. The trauma began when John received a frantic phone call from the hospital, informing him that his son had been rushed in after collapsing at work. The sheer intensity of the moment was overwhelming; the sound of sirens outside, the anxious looks from medical staff, and the continuous beeping of machines as they fought to stabilize his son’s condition. This experience has made John hypersensitive to any cues associated with hospitals, ambulances, or physical examinations. Since that time, John has gone out of his way to avoid anything medically related. He would often cancel appointments if he thought there was a chance of undergoing even the simplest medical procedure. His aversion extended beyond just himself; he also began avoiding family gatherings where there might be discussions about health issues, fearing it could trigger a relapse into those painful memories. To cope with the intrusive thoughts and memories that frequently surfaced, John developed strategies to keep his mind occupied all the time. He would immerse himself in work tasks, often staying late at the office or taking on extra projects just to ensure he was always busy. However, this constant need for distraction has taken a toll on his relationships, particularly with his colleagues who found him increasingly difficult to reach and less approachable. John had come to believe that if he hadn’t rushed his son to the hospital quickly enough, the outcome might have been different. The self-blame and guilt were overwhelming; he was certain that he should have protected his son more effectively and felt responsible for not doing so. These thoughts of failure and doubt permeated his daily life, making it nearly impossible to trust himself in high-pressure situations at work. The event has also left John with a heightened sense of threat and physical reactivity. Whenever something took longer than expected—be it a meeting running over or a delayed response from a client—he would immediately assume the worst and experience strong physical reactions such as breathlessness and intense fear. These symptoms often led to him feeling agitated and anxious, further exacerbating his tendency to avoid situations where he felt vulnerable. John’s avoidance behaviors have not only affected his personal life but also his professional responsibilities. He has missed several important deadlines due to his constant state of anxiety and the fear of something going wrong. His colleagues noticed a decline in his performance and began to question his reliability, which further fueled John's self-doubt and sense of failure. It was during one particularly stressful project deadline that John finally realized he needed help. He had been so consumed by his avoidance strategies and the constant fear of something bad happening again that he could no longer function effectively at work or enjoy any semblance of a normal life. The fear of reliving those harrowing moments and the guilt over not being able to protect his son drove him to seek therapy. John is now most afraid of losing control, both personally and professionally, and hopes that with help, he can find a way to manage his symptoms without letting them dictate his every move. He is looking for strategies to cope with his intrusive thoughts and triggers so that he can regain the confidence and peace of mind he once had.
